steps.what: Secure the property: lock, forward mail

pieces.text: Ask if a prepaid funeral plan exists. Many people have one and never mention it.

alt: A timeline card of the first 48 hours after a parent dies, from getting the death pronounced to securing the property, beside a note about prepaid funeral plans.
caption: The first 48 hours, in order. The rest of the two weeks follows in the guide.

line2: in the order it is done

steps.what: Get the medical cause of death certificate
Register the death: 5 days, 8 in Scotland

pieces.eyebrow: Who to tell in two weeks
items: Tell Us Once, via the registrar

alt: A timeline of the first days after a death in the UK, from the medical certificate to the funeral director, beside a short checklist of who to tell.
caption: The registration deadline is five days in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, and eight in Scotland.

pieces.text: Keep the post for at least a year. Annual statements find accounts no one knew about.

alt: A table of what regular outgoings, incomings, annual payments and small recurring amounts in twelve months of bank statements can reveal, with a note to keep the post.
caption: Bank statements leave the clearest trail. The guide lists the other places to look.

items: A safe deposit box, if any
A will register, where one exists

pieces.text: Read the executor clause first. That person has the authority to act.

alt: A checklist of places to look for a will, from home to the lawyer, a deposit box, a will register and the executor, beside a note to read the executor clause first.
caption: Work down the list rather than across it: each place takes more effort than the one before.

pieces.question: You were named executor. What now?
options: Serve, following the steps in order

pieces.text: Wait out your state's creditor claim period before you distribute anything.

alt: A choice card listing the options for someone named executor: serve, bring in a probate attorney, or decline before acting, beside a note about creditor claim periods.
caption: You can decline formally, as long as you have not started acting as executor.

items: The original will, not a copy
Details of any funeral plan paid

pieces.text: Look for creditors before you distribute anything. Executors can be personally liable.

alt: A checklist of what an executor should ask for immediately, from certified certificates to the original will and bank statements, with a note about creditors.
caption: You can decline, as long as you have not already started acting as executor.

line2: A map of where it all is

pieces.text: No passwords, PINs or full account numbers. Write where things are, not what they are.

alt: A blank printable page titled If something happens to me, with lines for the will, banks, pensions, insurance, property and anything that would surprise someone.
caption: The lines a file like this holds. Locations and references only, never the credentials.

pieces.text: Ask each provider who is currently named. They will tell you.

alt: A table showing how a pension, life insurance, a joint bank account and a sole account usually pass on, and whether the will controls each, beside a note.
caption: Generalized, and details vary by country and provider. Not legal advice.

items: Which bank, and what is due out
Where rent or mortgage is paid
Where keys and the alarm code are

pieces.text: Locations and references, not logins. Safe to leave in a drawer.

alt: A checklist of what someone would need in the first two weeks of running your life, from the bank and rent to keys, alarm code and who to call, with a note.
caption: Two weeks, not forever: a list you can write in one sitting.

pieces.text: Set a legacy contact where it is offered. It takes minutes.

alt: A table of what usually happens to email, photo storage, subscriptions and cryptocurrency after a death, and what helps, beside a note about legacy contacts.
caption: Policies change and vary by country, so treat this as a starting point.

pieces.eyebrow: Roughly how long to keep things

pieces.text: One thin emergency folder, one for active paperwork, one archive box.

alt: A table of how long to keep certificates, property deeds, tax records and bills, beside a note on sorting into emergency, active and archive.
caption: General guidance. Tax retention rules vary by country, so check yours.

lines.label: Say
lines.text: I have been sorting my own paperwork. No one would know where mine is.

lines.label: Then
lines.text: If you were both in hospital for two weeks, I would not know where to start.

lines.label: Ask
lines.text: Where is the will kept? Which bank? Who is the lawyer?

pieces.text: The will's location this month, the pensions next month.

alt: A script card with three ways to open the conversation with a parent about their affairs, starting with your own paperwork, beside a note to go slowly.
caption: Example wording. Ask for locations, not contents.

pieces.caption: Who to call, the will, the email address. One evening.

alt: A compare card of what to write in a life admin binder and what to leave out, beside a card suggesting three pages as a start.
caption: Write where something is, not what it says.

pieces.eyebrow: What would someone need to find?

pieces.caption: Long enough to show the gaps, short enough to write in one go.

alt: A table of four questions someone would ask if you were in the hospital for two weeks, with what to write down for each, beside a card on why two weeks is a good size.
caption: Answer with where, not what.

pieces.eyebrow: Two roles, one or two people

pieces.text: Ask them before you write their name down, and name a second person.

alt: A compare card of an emergency contact and a medical decision maker, two roles that can be one person or two, beside a note to ask first and name a second person.
caption: Not legal or medical advice. The formal documents vary by state.

pieces.eyebrow: If I could not raise them
pieces.title: My choice, on one page

pieces.text: A name that would say no is worse than no name.

alt: A blank printable page for recording who you would want to raise your children, with a second choice, the details of a normal week and where paperwork is kept.
caption: The human side of the choice. Confirm the legal side with an attorney in your state.

steps.what: Close family, told by a person
Funeral team and whoever handles affairs
Employer, banks and insurers, by phone

pieces.text: Keep one page of who you told, when, and what they need next.

alt: A timeline of who to tell when someone dies, from close family first to utilities and subscriptions when you have the energy, beside a note to keep a log.
caption: Most of the list is not urgent.

line2: Now what is out of date

pieces.text: A divorce does not necessarily change who is named on a form by itself.

alt: A table matching life events such as a move, a marriage, a new child or a new job to the paperwork worth looking at again, beside a note about names on forms.
caption: Where to look, not what to do. Ask the provider or an attorney.

items: What it is: safe, box or lockbox
Who can open it: a name, no code

pieces.text: Write who has the key or where the instructions are, not the instructions.

alt: A checklist of three things to write down about a safe or deposit box, what it is, where it is and who can open it, beside a note never to record the combination.
caption: Say where, not what.

items: Vet name and where records are
A backup if the first cannot

pieces.text: A person who agreed is a plan. A name on a page is a hope.

alt: A checklist for a pet care note, covering who would take each animal, food and medication, the vet, papers and a backup, beside a note about asking first.
caption: A few minutes per animal.
